solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Ten shillings for Mary?

definitions.meaning: before decimal coinage a sovereign was a gold pound coin of twenty shillings, so ten shillings was half of it
Mary II reigned jointly with William III, so she was one of two monarchs sharing the throne

explanation.surface: A question about what ten shillings meant to someone called Mary, perhaps her pocket money.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is whimsical: William and Mary ruled together, so Mary was half the monarch. The question mark flags the pun. Ten shillings was half a pound in old British money.
explanation.definitionFit: Both readings fit the phrase: half a gold pound coin equals ten shillings, and a joint queen was literally half of the ruling monarch.

clue.text: Fluid state of matter

definitions.meaning: the pale liquid part of blood, in which the cells float
the ionised gas counted as a fourth state alongside solid, liquid and gas

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the liquid portion of blood and the ionised-gas phase studied in physics.

clue.text: Maybe stand in a queue at ground level for cosmetic treatment

definitions.text: Maybe stand in a queue at ground level
definitions.meaning: someone waiting on the ground floor for an elevator would turn toward it, i.e. face the lift
surgery that tightens the skin of the face

explanation.surface: Waiting in line on the ground floor somehow leads to a beauty procedure.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the answer into two words: to face (look towards) the lift (British for elevator) while queuing on the ground floor.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosmetic surgery that tightens sagging facial skin is the standard name of this procedure.

clue.text: Fitting in living quarters

definitions.meaning: adjusting to suit others, as in reaching an arrangement or compromise
rooms or lodgings where people stay

explanation.definitionFit: The noun covers both adapting to circumstances and the lodging someone is given to live in.

clue.text: Like some music that could be rendered by an alto

indicators.note: a piece rendered is performed or recast, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Describes music that an alto singer might perform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be rendered' tells us to rearrange the letters of 'an alto'.
explanation.definitionFit: Music without a key centre, such as Schoenberg's, is described as lacking tonality.

clue.text: Virtuous girl, then the reverse of very good, in a state

indicators.note: says the letters for very good are written backwards

parts.note: A1, written AI in crosswords, means first-rate

explanation.surface: A tale of a good girl who then turns out to be the opposite of very good, somewhere in a US state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the reverse of' turns AI (A1, top quality) into IA. 'in a' just links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of the fifty American states, on the east coast.

clue.text: Association of everyone that is kept outside particular African party

indicators.note: the abbreviation for 'that is' wraps around the African party

parts.note: i.e., the Latin abbreviation id est
the ANC, South Africa's African National Congress

explanation.surface: A grouping of everyone, apart from one African political party that is excluded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kept outside' looks like exclusion, but it means the abbreviation for 'that is' wraps round the party. ANC is South Africa's African National Congress.
explanation.definitionFit: An alliance is a union or league of parties, a synonym for an association.

clue.text: Central area that would be a success if provided with pub

indicators.note: the answer plus the pub abbreviation would make the phrase for success, so that abbreviation is what the phrase lacks

parts.note: a triumph is a great success
PH is the map abbreviation for public house

explanation.surface: A central space that would make a hit if a pub were added to it.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards: add PH (public house) to the answer and you get A TRIUMPH, so the answer is A TRIUMPH with PH removed.
explanation.definitionFit: An atrium is the open central court or hall of a building, or a heart chamber.

clue.text: Dad less good, we deduce, as a religious leader

definitions.meaning: if the father is inferior, the logical inference is that the other parent ranks above him
the head of a convent of nuns

explanation.surface: From finding a father wanting we reach a conclusion about a church figure.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is playful logic: father inferior, therefore the other parent is the better one.
explanation.definitionFit: The title belongs to the nun who heads a convent, a female leader in a religious community.

clue.text: In the wake of micro-organism there's a nameless horrible disease

indicators.note: the rearranged letters follow behind the microbe
something horrible is a mess, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: After a microbe spreads, an unnamed nasty illness follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'horrible' rearranges A NAMELESS, and 'In the wake of' puts the result after the microbe.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubella, a mild viral infection causing a rash, is commonly known by this name.

clue.text: Fool sitting in cafe's terrible

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters across these words

explanation.surface: A clown in a café is said to be awful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sitting in' points to the letters hidden across CAFE'S TERRIBLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Feste is the jester in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, a professional fool.

clue.text: Very quickly sir loses head when meeting maiden?

parts.note: in cricket a maiden is an over in which no runs are scored, so it is one kind of over

indicators.note: the first letter of the titled man is dropped

parts.note: a knight is addressed as Sir

explanation.surface: A knight hastily loses his head on meeting a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maiden' looks like a young woman but is a cricket term: a maiden over, six balls with no runs. The question mark marks it as an example of OVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatically, something happening overnight happens suddenly, almost instantly.

clue.text: It's mud that's nasty outside a sporting arena

indicators.note: the rearranged letters surround the single letter that follows
letters made nasty are messed up, so this pair of words is rearranged

explanation.surface: A grumble that the mud outside a sports ground is unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's nasty' rearranges IT'S MUD into STDIUM, which goes 'outside' A.
explanation.definitionFit: A stadium is a large venue with tiers of seating for watching games and athletics.

clue.text: This writer with way that includes good bits and bobs

parts.note: the setter referring to themself as me

indicators.note: the road word takes in the letter for good

parts.note: a lane is a road or way

explanation.surface: The setter, on a road, finds a pleasant assortment of odds and ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is a standard crossword way of saying ME.
explanation.definitionFit: A mélange is a mixture or medley, much like a jumble of odds and ends.

clue.text: Invalid aunts are terrible hypochondriacs?

indicators.note: letters described as terrible are in a bad state, so they get rearranged

explanation.surface: Sick aunts are awful worriers about their health.
explanation.walkthrough: Careful: 'are' belongs in the fodder too. Rearrange INVALID AUNTS ARE; the indicator is 'terrible'. The question mark admits that invalids are not necessarily imagining their ills.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes people anxiously preoccupied with their own health, close to those who imagine illness.

clue.text: Classics expert least likely to get money, I gathered

indicators.note: the outer word gathers up the money word and the I inside it

parts.note: last, as in the last person you would expect
tin is old slang for money

explanation.surface: A scholar of the classics is the person least likely to get rich, or so I hear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I gathered' reads as 'I understood', but 'gathered' says money and I are taken inside the word for least likely. Tin is old British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latinist is a scholar of the Latin language and literature, a classicist.

clue.text: Cleric always getting to tear around

indicators.note: the tearing word goes around the word for always

parts.note: to rend is to tear apart
ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'

explanation.surface: A clergyman who is constantly rushing about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tear around' reads as dashing about, but 'tear' is the ripping sense and 'around' makes it enclose the word for always.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is the courtesy form used for clergy, so it also stands for a member of the clergy.

clue.text: Terry wants edges taken off mechanical device

indicators.note: the surname loses its first and last letters

parts.note: Terry Pratchett, the British author of the Discworld fantasy novels

explanation.surface: Someone called Terry wants the rough edges smoothed off a machine part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terry' is Sir Terry Pratchett, the British fantasy novelist; trimming both ends of his surname with 'edges taken off' leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratchet is a toothed wheel or bar with a pawl allowing motion in one direction only.

clue.text: We hear journalist will fly

indicators.note: the answer is said like the words for the journalist plus his contracted will

parts.note: a hack is a journalist, and 'will' is shortened to 'll, so the phrase is hack'll

explanation.surface: Rumour has it a reporter is going to take a flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fly' looks like a verb but is a noun: an angler's artificial fly made with feathers. 'We hear' marks the sound-alike of HACK'LL.
explanation.definitionFit: In angling, a hackle is an artificial fishing lure dressed with a cock's neck feathers.

clue.text: Wrap new novel in bits of expensive paper

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go inside the two initials
small pieces, here the leading letter of each of the two words
made new, so the letters of the word that follows are reworked

explanation.surface: Gift-wrapping a new book in pricey paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges NOVEL into NVELO, which goes 'in' E and P, the 'bits of' expensive paper.
explanation.definitionFit: To envelop is to cover or surround completely, just as wrapping encloses something.

clue.text: Irritable in uniform

definitions.meaning: bad-tempered, as if suffering a liver complaint
the distinctive dress of servants or a guild

explanation.surface: A person in uniform who is touchy.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means testy (from a sluggish liver), and the noun is the special dress worn by retainers or company members.

clue.text: Tricky course half abandoned with unions becoming harmless

indicators.note: tricky suggests something awkward and twisted, so the letters are jumbled
the second half of the word is dropped, keeping its first three letters

explanation.surface: A difficult course, half given up when trade unions step in, turns out to be harmless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half abandoned' keeps COU from COURSE; 'Tricky' shuffles COU with UNIONS. 'becoming' just links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Innocuous describes something that causes no injury or offence, a synonym of harmless.

clue.text: Don is one person at the wheel heading off

definitions.note: the Don flows through Yorkshire (and another through Russia), so it is an example

indicators.note: the first letter is removed

explanation.surface: A university don counts as a person in charge, setting off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like a university teacher or a man's name; it is a river, such as the Don in Yorkshire or Russia.
explanation.definitionFit: The Don is a watercourse, so it is one example of this kind of flowing water.

clue.text: Move into comfortable position as multinational company

definitions.meaning: the Swiss food and drinks giant behind Nescafé and KitKat

explanation.surface: Settling in snugly as a big global firm might in a new market.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to settle snugly, and the same letters name the Swiss food conglomerate.

clue.text: A lord, one unlikely to be an artist

indicators.note: an unlikely arrangement is an improbable one, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A peer who seems an improbable candidate for a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unlikely' rearranges A LORD ONE; 'to be an' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo da Vinci, the Renaissance painter of the Mona Lisa, is a famous example.
